summary: The bill directs the HHS Secretary to create and annually update a National Plan for Epilepsy that coordinates all federal research, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care efforts, while establishing a public advisory council to issue biennial recommendations and requiring annual progress reports to Congress.

scores.thoughts: The bill establishes a new National Plan for Epilepsy under the Public Health Service Act, creates an ongoing Advisory Council, mandates annual assessments and reports, and requires federal coordination across agencies. These activities necessarily involve new or expanded federal administrative and programmatic spending, even without specified appropriations. This is a moderate, direct expansion of government activity and outlays.
The bill contains no provisions related to tax policy, rates, credits, or revenue measures.

The legislation directly mandates federal coordination of epilepsy research, prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care delivery through HHS agencies (NIH, CDC, CMS, FDA, HRSA). It emphasizes improving early diagnosis, care coordination, access to specialized care, and reducing health disparities—all core healthcare system functions. This constitutes moderate federal/public-sector engagement in healthcare.
No provisions address firearms, regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border policy, or related protections.
No provisions address reproductive health services or abortion access.
The bill includes DoD and VA representatives on the Advisory Council for coordination purposes only; it does not alter defense budgets, programs, or policy.
No provisions relate to environmental regulation, climate policy, or conservation.
The findings note employment and income effects of epilepsy, but the bill itself creates no new welfare, SNAP, or income-support programs.
No provisions address schools, school choice, federal education funding, or curriculum.
No provisions address controlled substances, decriminalization, or enforcement.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.
By authorizing new federal planning, reporting, and coordination activities, the bill implies modest additional deficit-financed spending; however, the connection is indirect and secondary.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance or international aid programs.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or voter ID.
No provisions address technology regulation, data privacy, or surveillance.
No provisions address collective bargaining, worker protections, or union rules.
No provisions address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination law.
